title: Rate Limiting
subtitle: Watch a flood of requests hit a limiter, and see how buckets, windows and Redis keep one client from starving everyone else.
learn: How a token bucket allows short bursts but caps the long-run rate
How a leaky bucket smooths traffic, and how it differs from a token bucket
Why fixed windows allow double bursts at the boundary and how sliding windows fix it
How to share counters across many servers with atomic Redis operations
Where to enforce limits and what to do when the limiter itself fails

steps.title: One client, all the capacity
steps.body: Our API service can comfortably handle about 200 requests per second. A buggy script in one customer's code suddenly sends 500 requests per second with the same API key. Nobody is attacking us, yet every other customer now sees timeouts. How do we stop one caller from using more than its fair share?
steps.idea: Rate limiting protects shared capacity by capping how much any one caller may consume.
steps.caption: The noisy client floods the gateway and the service.

steps.title: Token bucket
steps.body: Give each API key a bucket that holds up to 10 tokens and refills at 2 tokens per second. Every request must take one token, and if the bucket is empty the request is refused. A quiet client keeps a full bucket, so it can burst 10 requests at once; a steady client is held to 2 per second on average. Two numbers, capacity and refill rate, set burst size and sustained rate.
steps.idea: A token bucket permits bursts up to its capacity while enforcing a long-run average rate.
steps.caption: A normal client spends a token per request.

steps.title: Saying no cheaply
steps.body: The noisy client drains its 10 tokens in about 20 ms and then gets only the 2 refilled each second. The gateway answers the rest with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and a Retry-After header, without touching the service or database. Rejecting costs microseconds, while serving would cost real work. Good clients read Retry-After and back off.
steps.idea: Reject early and cheaply with 429 and Retry-After so excess load never reaches the expensive parts.
steps.caption: The gateway returns 429 to the noisy client.

steps.title: Leaky bucket
steps.body: A leaky bucket works like a queue with a hole: requests enter the bucket and drain out at a fixed rate, say 2 per second. If the bucket is full, new requests overflow and are dropped. The output to the service is perfectly smooth, which is useful when the downstream cannot tolerate bursts. The price is that bursts are delayed in the queue rather than served immediately.
steps.idea: Token bucket allows bursts through; leaky bucket flattens them into a constant outflow.
steps.caption: Requests drain to the service at a steady pace.

steps.title: Fixed vs sliding windows
steps.body: A simpler idea is a fixed window: allow 100 requests per minute and reset a counter at each minute boundary. The flaw is that a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, which is 200 in two seconds, double the limit. A sliding window log stores timestamps and is exact but costs memory. A sliding window counter blends the current and previous window counts, which is cheap and close enough.
steps.idea: Fixed windows are cheap but leak a 2x burst at the boundary; sliding windows close the gap at a small cost.
steps.caption: Two back-to-back windows let a 2x burst through.

steps.title: Shared counters in Redis
steps.body: Real gateways run as many instances behind a load balancer. If each keeps its own bucket, a limit of 100 per minute across 10 instances silently becomes up to 1000. So the buckets live in Redis, keyed by API key. The gateway runs one Lua script that reads the bucket, refills it from elapsed time, and takes a token atomically. A separate read then write would let two instances both see one token left and both spend it.
steps.idea: Keep counters in one shared store and update them atomically, or the limit multiplies by the instance count.
steps.caption: Every gateway instance asks Redis, which decides.

steps.title: Redis goes down
steps.body: Now the limiter's own dependency fails. If the gateway fails closed and rejects everything, a counter outage becomes a full outage. If it fails open and allows everything, we lose protection exactly when load may be high. A common compromise is to fall back to a coarse local limit per instance, accept some inaccuracy, and set a short timeout (a few milliseconds) on the Redis call so the limiter never slows requests. Here each instance falls back to a coarse local cap of about 20 requests per second for this key.
steps.idea: Decide the limiter's failure mode in advance: usually fail open or degrade to a local limit, never block all traffic.
steps.caption: Redis is unreachable; the gateway uses a local fallback.

steps.title: Where to enforce, and on what key
steps.body: Limits can sit at a CDN or edge, at the API gateway, or inside each service. Edge limits stop floods cheaply; gateway limits know the customer and plan; service limits protect a specific costly endpoint such as search or export. Choose the key carefully: per API key or user is fair, while per IP punishes everyone behind a shared office or mobile NAT address. Different endpoints and plans often get different limits.
steps.idea: Enforce as early as the identity is known, and pick a key that matches who you want to be fair to.
steps.caption: Limits apply at the gateway, with a stricter one in the service.

steps.title: Fair shares for everyone
steps.body: A token bucket allows bursts at a set average rate, and a leaky bucket smooths output. Fixed windows are simple but burst at the boundary, so prefer sliding windows when accuracy matters. With many servers, keep counters in Redis and update them atomically. Return 429 with Retry-After, decide how the limiter fails, and enforce at the earliest point that knows who the caller is.
steps.idea: Pick an algorithm for the burst behaviour you want, share state atomically, and plan for limiter failure.
steps.caption: The limiter shields the service from one noisy caller.

quiz.q: An API uses a token bucket with capacity 20 and a refill of 5 tokens per second. A client was idle for a minute, then sends 30 requests instantly. Roughly how many succeed?
quiz.why: The idle client has a full bucket of 20 tokens, so 20 succeed immediately. The other 10 are refused until tokens refill at 5 per second.

quiz.q: A limit of 60 requests per minute uses a fixed window. A client sends 60 requests at 10:00:59 and 60 more at 10:01:01. What happens?
options: Only 30 of the second batch pass
quiz.why: The counter resets at 10:01:00, so both batches fit in separate windows. This boundary burst is the main weakness of fixed windows.

quiz.q: Eight gateway instances each hold a local counter for a 100 per minute limit, and requests are spread evenly. What is the effective limit for one customer?
quiz.why: Each instance allows 100 on its own, so the combined limit can reach 8 x 100. Shared counters in Redis restore the real limit.

quiz.q: Why is the Redis rate-limit check done in a single Lua script rather than a GET followed by a SET?
options: Lua is faster than any other language
It makes the check and update atomic, so two instances cannot both spend the last token
Redis cannot do GET and SET separately
It avoids needing a key expiry
quiz.why: With separate commands, two gateways can both read 1 token left and both allow a request. A script runs without interleaving, closing that race.

quiz.q: Your limiter's Redis cluster is down during peak traffic. Which response is usually the best default?
options: Reject every request until Redis returns
Fall back to a coarse local limit with a short Redis timeout
Retry Redis in a loop until it answers
quiz.why: Failing closed turns a limiter outage into an outage of the whole API, and unlimited access removes protection. A local fallback keeps service up with approximate limits.

cheatsheet.def: Bucket of tokens refilled at a fixed rate; each request spends one. Allows bursts up to capacity, with a capped average rate.
Queue that drains at a constant rate and drops overflow. Produces smooth output but delays bursts.
Counter per time slice (for example per minute). Cheap, but can allow up to 2x the limit across a boundary.
Counts requests in the last N seconds. The log version is exact; the counter version weights the previous window and is approximate.
Use a Lua script (or INCR with EXPIRE set together) so read, refill and spend happen as one step across all instances.
HTTP status and header telling the client it was limited and when to try again. Reject before doing real work.
What you count by: API key, user, IP or endpoint. IP is crude because many users can share one address.
Whether requests pass or are blocked when the limiter cannot decide. Prefer fail open or a local fallback for availability.
